items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the following geometric sequence:
[MATH: 3,\quad 6,\quad 12,\quad 24, \quad \ldots]

Content:
Suppose we want to find the first term that exceeds [MATH: 3\,000\,000.] We can do this by creating and solving an inequality.

Content:
First, let's construct a formula for the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence. The first term of the sequence is [MATH: a_1=3,] and the common ratio is
[MATH: r = \dfrac 6 3 = 2.]

Content:
So, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence can be written as

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = 3 ⋅ 2^{n − 1}.]

Content:
We want the [MATH: n]th term to be greater than [MATH: 3\,000\,000.] So, we can set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|> 3000000; 3 ⋅ 2^{n − 1}|> 3000000; 2^{n − 1}|> 1000000; \log (2^{n − 1})|> \log (1000000); (n − 1)\log (2)|> \log (1000000); n − 1|> (\log (1000000))/(\log (2)); n|> (\log (1000000))/(\log (2)) + 1]

Content:
Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac {\log (1\,000\,000)} {\log (2)} + 1 \approx 20.932.]

Content:
Therefore, the [MATH: 21]st term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds [MATH: 3\,000\,000.]

Content:
To check our answer, we can easily verify that [MATH: a_{20} < 3\, 000\, 000] and [MATH: a_{21} > 3\, 000\, 000\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: a_{20}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{20 − 1} = 3 ⋅ 2^{19} = 1572864 < 3000000; a_{21}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{21 − 1} = 3 ⋅ 2^{20} = 3145728 > 3000000✓]

Content:
So, [MATH: a_{21}] is indeed the first term that exceeds [MATH: 3\,000\,000.]

sections.normalized_html: What is the first term that exceeds [MATH: 2\,000\,000] in the following geometric sequence? [MATH: \dfrac 1 {32},\: \dfrac 1 4,\: 2,\: 16,\: \ldots]
sections.readable_text:
What is the first term that exceeds [MATH: 2\,000\,000] in the following geometric sequence?
[MATH: \dfrac 1 {32},\: \dfrac 1 4,\: 2,\: 16,\: \ldots]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The first term of the sequence is [MATH: a_1=\dfrac{1}{32}] and the common ratio is [MATH: r = \dfrac {\left(\dfrac 1 {4}\right)} {\left(\dfrac 1 {32} \right)} = 8.]

So, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence can be written as follows:

[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = (1)/(32) ⋅ 8^{n − 1}; = (2)/(64) ⋅ 8^{n − 1}; = (2)/(8^{2}) ⋅ 8^{n − 1}; = 2 ⋅ 8^{− 2} ⋅ 8^{n − 1}; = 2 ⋅ 8^{n − 3}]

We want the [MATH: n]th term to be greater than [MATH: 2\,000\,000.] So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

[MATH: 2 ⋅ 8^{n − 3}|> 2000000; 8^{n − 3}|> 1000000; \log (8^{n − 3})|> \log (1000000); (n − 3)\log (8)|> \log (1000000); n − 3|> (\log (1000000))/(\log (8)); n|> (\log (1000000))/(\log (8)) + 3]

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get [MATH: \dfrac {\log (1\,000\, 000)} {\log (8)} + 3 \approx 9.643.]

Therefore, the [MATH: 10]th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds [MATH: 2\,000\,000.]

sections.normalized_html: What is the first term that is less than [MATH: 0. 000\,000\,1] in the following geometric sequence? [MATH: 16,\: 8,\: 4,\: 2,\: \ldots]
sections.readable_text:
What is the first term that is less than [MATH: 0. 000\,000\,1] in the following geometric sequence?
[MATH: 16,\: 8,\: 4,\: 2,\: \ldots]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The first term of the sequence is [MATH: a_1=16,] and the common ratio is [MATH: r = \dfrac 8 {16} = \dfrac 1 2.]

So, the [MATH: n]th term of the sequence can be written as

[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} ⋅ r^{n − 1}; = 16 ⋅ ((1)/(2))^{n − 1}; = 2^{4} ⋅ 2^{1 − n}; = 2^{5 − n}.]

We want the [MATH: n]th term to be less than [MATH: 0.000\,000\,1.] So, we set up and solve the corresponding inequality:

[MATH: 2^{5 − n}|< 0.0000001; \log (2^{5 − n})|< \log (0.0000001); 5 − n|< (\log (0.0000001))/(\log (2)); − n|< (\log (0.0000001))/(\log (2)) − 5; n|> 5 − (\log (0.0000001))/(\log (2))]

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get

[MATH: 5 - \dfrac { \log (0.000\, 000\, 1)} {\log (2)} \approx 28.253.]

Therefore, the [MATH: 29]th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than [MATH: 0. 000\,000\,1.]
